newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Hundreds of Albanian investors clash with police.
newsitem.headline: Hundreds of Albanian investors clash with police.

text.p: Hundreds of angry protestors demanding their money back from a get-rich-quick pyramid scheme battled Albanian riot police on Wednesday, eyewitnesses said.

About 500 demonstrators broke away from a crowd of 5,000 that had gathered outside the offices of the Sude pyramid scheme in western Tirana and set off to march two kilometres (just over a mile) to the capital's main Skanderbeg Square.
They hurled stones at around 50 police wielding batons who blocked their progress. Several arrests were made.

"We want our money back. (President) Sali Berisha you are a thief. (Prime Minister Aleksander) Meksi you are a thief. Down with the dictatorship," the crowd chanted, directing much anger against the Balkan country's political leadership.

Pyramid schemes, offering returns of up to 200 percent over three months, have sprung up across the impoverished Balkan state since the fall of communism in 1991. Sude ceased making repayments to depositors in November.
"First they stole our votes and now they are trying to steal our money," one woman said, accusing the ruling Democratic Party of failing to keep its election promises of security and prosperity.
The opposition Socialists have slammed Berisha for turning a blind eye to the pyramid schemes and plunging Albania into an economic crisis. On Wednesday it called for mass demonstrations.
Police, joined by reinforcements, were in no mood to make way for the protesters. "Look what they have done to us," said an elderly man, bearing a neck wound he said was inflicted by a police baton.
Frustrated by police blockades in their attempts to enter Skanderbeg Square, about 200 demonstrators chose instead to occupy a main road circling central Tirana, bringing traffic to a standstill.
Police did not intervene with the sit-in but massive forces were on alert in roads leading to Skanderbeg Square and police director Arben Prrenjasi also attended the scene.
"It's a big problem for us too because about three-quarters of police have put their money in pyramid schemes," a high-ranking police official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said.

The target of Wednesday's demonstration, Sude, is run by Maksude Kademi, a 30-year-old Romany gypsy woman, but it is only one of myriad such schemes in the company. One company collapsed last year and four others have temporarily suspended payments.
The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank have both expressed concern at the spread of the shemes but the government has been slow to act against them.
